claim: Aberrant liquid-to-solid phase transitions of biomolecular condensates have been linked to various neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Aberrant liquid-to-solid phase transitions of biomolecular condensates have been linked to various neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the context of the manuscript and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Misfolding of the RNA recognition motif of FUS is a key driver of condensate aging.
source: We identify misfolding of the RNA recognition motif of FUS as a key driver of condensate aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including XL-MS and aging experiments.

claim: HspB8 partitions into FUS condensates via its intrinsically disordered domain.
source: We demonstrate that the small heat shock protein HspB8 partitions into FUS condensates via its intrinsically disordered domain
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from partitioning experiments with HspB8 truncation variants.

claim: HspB8 prevents condensate hardening via condensate-specific interactions that are mediated by its α-crystallin domain.
source: We demonstrate that the small heat shock protein HspB8 partitions into FUS condensates via its intrinsically disordered domain and prevents condensate hardening via condensate-specific interactions that are mediated by its α-crystallin domain (αCD).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from aging assays and XL-MS experiments showing αCD-RRM interactions.

claim: The αCD-mediated interactions are altered in a disease-associated mutant of HspB8 (K141E).
source: These αCD-mediated interactions are altered in a disease-associated mutant of HspB8, which abrogates the ability of HspB8 to prevent condensate hardening.
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data comparing HspB8-WT and HspB8-K141E mutant.

claim: The HspB8-K141E mutant abrogates the ability of HspB8 to prevent condensate hardening.
source: These αCD-mediated interactions are altered in a disease-associated mutant of HspB8, which abrogates the ability of HspB8 to prevent condensate hardening.
evidence: This is supported by aging assays and FRAP experiments showing loss of chaperone activity.

claim: Liquid condensates can harden and evolve into less dynamic states with reduced fluidity and protein movement.
source: Liquid condensates can harden and evolve into less dynamic states with reduced fluidity and protein movement, leading to fibrillar assemblies that are often associated with disease (Aguzzi and Altmeyer, 2016; Patel et al., 2015; Molliex et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Stress granules are composed of RNA and translation factors.
source: Stress granules are composed of RNA and translation factors (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Sanders et al., 2020; Jain et al., 2016; Markmiller et al., 2018; Youn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The ability of stress granule proteins to phase separate forms the basis for stress granule assembly.
source: There is an increasing body of evidence that the ability of stress granule proteins to phase separate forms the basis for stress granule assembly (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Purified stress granule residing RNA-binding proteins phase separate into liquid droplets in vitro.
source: For instance, purified stress granule residing RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) phase separate into liquid droplets in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Reconstituted droplets have physicochemical properties similar to stress granules in cells.
source: Reconstituted droplets have physicochemical properties similar to stress granules in cells (Patel et al., 2015; Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In vitro reconstituted molecular condensates are metastable and age into less dynamic amorphous drops and fibrillar aggregates with time.
source: In vitro reconstituted molecular condensates are metastable and age into less dynamic amorphous drops, and fibrillar aggregates with time (Patel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The molecular aging process is accelerated by ALS-linked mutations in FUS and other RBPs.
source: Notably, the molecular aging process is accelerated by ALS-linked mutations in FUS and other RBPs (Patel et al., 2015; Molliex et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Small heat shock proteins have been shown to accumulate in stress granules that undergo an aberrant conversion from a liquid to a solid-like state.
source: sHSPs have been shown to accumulate in stress granules that undergo an aberrant conversion from a liquid to a solid-like state (Mateju et al., 2017; Ganassi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and folded α-crystallin domain (αCD) of sHSPs contribute to their chaperone activity.
source: These ATP-independent chaperones hold unfolded proteins in a refolding-competent state and both their intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and folded α-crystallin domain (αCD) contribute to this activity (Haslbeck et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Phase separation of FUS family proteins is driven by multivalent interactions among tyrosine residues within its LCD and arginine residues of their RBDs.
source: It has been shown that phase separation of FUS family proteins is driven by multivalent interactions among tyrosine residues within its LCD and arginine residues of their RBDs (Qamar et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Schuster et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: At least part of the LCD of FUS can assemble into amyloid fibrils.
source: At least part of the LCD of FUS can assemble into amyloid fibrils (Murray et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The isolated FUS-LCD can adopt a hydrogel-like state that depends on amyloid-like interactions.
source: and the isolated FUS-LCD can adopt a hydrogel-like state that also depends on amyloid-like interactions (Kato et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The LCD appears to be disordered in liquid droplets, exhibiting no detectable secondary structure.
source: By contrast, the LCD appears to be disordered in liquid droplets, exhibiting no detectable secondary structure (Murthy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The isolated FUS-RRM has been shown to spontaneously self-assemble into amyloid fibrils.
source: In addition to the LCD, the isolated FUS-RRM has been shown to spontaneously self-assemble into amyloid fibrils (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Multiple intra-links within the RRM domain of FUSm increased inside the condensates.
source: The most prominent feature we detected after FUSm condensation was that multiple intra-links within the RRM domain of FUSm increased inside the condensates.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative XL-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was an increase in homo-dimeric links between RRM domains, indicative of interactions between RRM domains of different FUSm molecules.
source: In addition, there was an increase in homo-dimeric links between RRM domains, indicative of interactions between RRM domains of different FUSm molecules.
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Links between the RRM domain and the nuclear localization sequence (NLS) were increased.
source: Additionally, links between the RRM domain and the nuclear localization sequence (NLS) were increased
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Links within the Zinc-finger domain were decreased.
source: while links within the Zinc-finger domain were decreased (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: FUSm (FUS-G156E) shows an increased propensity for aggregation in vitro and in vivo.
source: It has been shown previously that FUSm (FUS-G156E) shows an increased propensity for aggregation in vitro and in vivo (Nomura et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Crosslinks within the RRM that were increased during condensation also change during molecular aging and particularly during fiber formation.
source: A closer examination focusing on those crosslinks within the RRM that were increased during condensation shows that these also change during molecular aging and particularly during fiber formation (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved XL-MS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The link within the RRM bridging positions 339 and 362 decreases as fibers form.
source: For instance, the link within the RRM bridging positions 339 and 362 decreases as fibers form.
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved XL-MS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HspB8 was sequestered into reconstituted FUSm condensates.
source: We find that HspB8 was sequestered into reconstituted FUSm condensates (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HspB8 fluorescence signal superimposed with the FUSm-GFP signal.
source: and that its fluorescence signal superimposed with the FUSm-GFP signal (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity plot profile shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HspB8 did not form droplets on its own under these conditions.
source: while it did not form droplets on its own under these conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HspB1 did not accumulate inside FUSm droplets.
source: Another closely related sHSP that has been localized to stress granules (Mateju et al., 2017), HspB1, did not accumulate inside FUSm droplets (Figure 2C, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: The concentration of HspB8 inside FUSm condensates was determined to be 2.4 mM.
source: Using the fluorescence signal of labeled HspB8 and a calibration curve, we determined the concentration of HspB8 inside FUSm condensates to be 2.4 mM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence calibration data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Inter-links predominantly formed inside the dense phase of the condensates.
source: Inter-links (crosslinks between different proteins) predominantly formed inside the dense phase of the condensates (Figure 2E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: HspB8 specifically binds to FUSm inside and not outside condensates.
source: Together with data from thermophoresis binding experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), this suggests that HspB8 specifically binds to FUSm inside and not outside condensates.
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data and thermophoresis experiments shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The majority of inter-links within the droplets were formed between the αCD of HspB8 and the RRM of FUSm.
source: We find the majority of inter-links within the droplets were formed between the αCD of HspB8 and the RRM of FUSm, and to a lesser degree the FUS-NLS.
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In the presence of HspB8, FUSm retained its liquidity over a time span of 24 hr.
source: A time-course experiment using photobleaching recovery (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching [FRAP]) revealed that in the presence of HspB8, FUSm retained its liquidity over a time span of 24 hr (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: FUSm droplets were able to fuse even after 6 hr in the presence of HspB8.
source: FUSm droplets were able to fuse even after 6 hr (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by optical tweezer experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The relaxation times of the fusion events were not affected by HspB8.
source: the relaxation times of the fusion events were not affected (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is supported by optical tweezer data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: HspB8 protects fresh FUSm condensates from converting into fibers.
source: In addition to protecting fresh FUSm condensates from converting into fibers (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: HspB8 prevented further conversion of pre-aged FUSm droplets and prevented seeding of fiber growth.
source: the chaperone prevented further conversion of pre-aged FUSm droplets, and prevented seeding of fiber growth (Figure 3G, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3G and Video 1.

claim: The protective effect of HspB8 on FUSm was also observed at sub-stoichiometric HspB8 concentrations.
source: The protective effect of HspB8 on FUSm was also observed at sub-stoichiometric HspB8 concentrations (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by aging assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: HspB8 binds to the FUS-RRM also during prolonged incubation times via the αCD::RRM interface established during condensation.
source: Our data show that HspB8 binds to the FUS-RRM also during prolonged incubation times via the αCD::RRM interface established during condensation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H & I).
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: HspB8 is likely to be significantly more disordered than the closely related HspB1.
source: Disorder prediction and circular dichroism analysis revealed that HspB8 is likely to be significantly more disordered than the closely related HspB1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by disorder prediction and circular dichroism data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The IDR-SNAP fusion construct was still recruited to FUSm condensates.
source: While the IDR-SNAP fusion construct was still recruited to FUSm condensates
evidence: This is supported by partitioning data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The αCD-SNAP variant no longer partitioned into FUSm condensates.
source: the αCD-SNAP variant no longer partitioned (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by partitioning data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The IDR-SNAP construct was not active in preventing FUSm fiber formation.
source: The IDR-SNAP construct was also not active in preventing FUSm fiber formation (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by aging assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The αCD-SNAP construct showed slight activity at high concentrations in preventing FUSm fiber formation.
source: while the αCD-SNAP construct showed slight activity at high concentrations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by aging assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The HspB8-IDR interacts with the FUS-LCD.
source: A partitioning analysis of these variants with droplets formed only by the LCD of FUS (AA1–211) under crowding conditions revealed a similar partitioning pattern as compared to the full-length FUSm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), indicating that the HspB8-IDR interacts with the FUS-LCD.
evidence: This is inferred from partitioning data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Partitioning of HspB8 was significantly reduced for FUS condensates formed by the 17 Y variant.
source: Partitioning of HspB8 was significantly reduced for FUS condensates formed by the 17 Y variant (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by partitioning data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tyrosines in the FUS-LCD interact with HspB8.
source: Partitioning of HspB8 was significantly reduced for FUS condensates formed by the 17 Y variant (Figure 4D), suggesting that tyrosines in the FUS-LCD interact with HspB8.
evidence: This is inferred from partitioning data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The 0 R variant of HspB8 did not accumulate in FUSm droplets in vitro.
source: This variant did not accumulate in FUSm droplets in vitro (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is supported by partitioning data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The 0 R variant of HspB8 did not partition into stress granules in cells.
source: and did not partition into stress granules in cells, contrary to the behavior of HspB8-WT (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The ability of the 0 R variant of HspB8 to prevent fiber formation was completely abolished.
source: When we tested the 0 R variant of HspB8 in a FUSm aging assay we found that its ability to prevent fiber formation was completely abolished (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by aging assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Deletion of the RRM domain in FUSm∆RRM significantly slowed down aging.
source: Deletion of the RRM domain in FUSm∆RRM significantly slowed down aging and first aggregates were observed after 36 hr.
evidence: This is supported by aging assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HspB8 was not able to prevent aging of the FUSm∆RRM variant.
source: Remarkably, HspB8 was not able to prevent aging of the FUSm∆RRM variant, indicating that HspB8 binding to the FUS-RRM is required for HspB8 to act as a chaperone for FUS.
evidence: This is supported by aging assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HspB8 binding to the FUS-RRM is required for HspB8 to act as a chaperone for FUS.
source: Remarkably, HspB8 was not able to prevent aging of the FUSm∆RRM variant, indicating that HspB8 binding to the FUS-RRM is required for HspB8 to act as a chaperone for FUS.
evidence: This is inferred from aging assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The majority of inter-links between FUSm and HspB8 that were significantly increased within condensates formed between the αCD of HspB8 and the RRM of FUSm.
source: Our XL-MS data shows that the majority of inter-links between FUSm and HspB8 that were significantly increased within condensates in fact formed between the αCD of HspB8 and the RRM of FUSm (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The melting temperature of the isolated FUS-RRM has been reported to be 52°C.
source: The melting temperature of the isolated FUS-RRM has been reported to be 52°C (Lu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Full-length FUSm formed amorphous aggregates after cooling down from heat shock.
source: While full-length FUSm formed amorphous aggregates after cooling down from heat shock, the FUSm∆RRM variant condensed into spherical droplets (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The FUSm∆RRM variant condensed into spherical droplets after cooling down from heat shock.
source: While full-length FUSm formed amorphous aggregates after cooling down from heat shock, the FUSm∆RRM variant condensed into spherical droplets (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Unfolding of the RRM domain is an integral part of the aging process.
source: This result strongly suggests that unfolding of the RRM domain is an integral part of the aging process
evidence: This is inferred from heat shock experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Deletion of the RRM prevents temperature-induced aggregation of FUSm condensates.
source: and deletion of the RRM prevents temperature-induced aggregation of FUSm condensates.
evidence: This is supported by heat shock experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: RNA can bind to the FUS-RRM and prevent aging of FUS.
source: It has been shown that RNA can bind to the FUS-RRM, prevent aging of FUS and dissolve condensates at high concentrations (Kramer et al., 2014; Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The addition of RNA led to a significant decrease in the number of detected inter-links between FUSm and HspB8.
source: While the addition of RNA led to a significant decrease in the number of detected inter-links between FUSm and HspB8, it did not alter the number of intra-links within FUSm or HspB8 (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: RNA and HspB8 can compete for binding to FUSm.
source: This result suggests that RNA and HspB8 can compete for binding to FUSm
evidence: This is inferred from XL-MS data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mutations of the lysine 141 residue in the αCD of HspB8 have been associated with Charcot-Marie Tooth disease.
source: Mutations of the lysine 141 residue in the αCD of HspB8 have been associated with Charcot-Marie Tooth disease, a currently incurable dominant autosomal disorder of the peripheral nervous system leading to muscular dystrophies (Irobi et al., 2004; Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Experimental evidence indicates a decreased chaperone activity for HspB8-K141E.
source: The mechanistic cause of the disease is still enigmatic, although experimental evidence indicates a decreased chaperone activity for HspB8-K141E (Kim et al., 2006; Carra et al., 2010; Carra et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HspB8-K141E still partitioned into reconstituted FUSm droplets.
source: when we tested HspB8-K141E for localization to FUSm droplets, we found that it still partitioned into reconstituted FUSm droplets (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by partitioning data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HspB8-K141E could not prevent FUSm aging.
source: While the HspB8 WT was active in a FUSm aging experiment, HspB8-K141E could not prevent FUSm aging (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is supported by aging assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The HspB8-K141E mutant exerted a dominant-negative effect over the WT, preventing the WT from being active.
source: and when mixed with the WT, the mutant exerted a dominant-negative effect over the WT, preventing the WT from being active.
evidence: This is supported by aging assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The HspB8-K141E mutant was much less effective compared to the WT in keeping FUSm in a dynamic state.
source: By using FRAP, we found that the mutant was much less effective compared to the WT in keeping FUSm in a dynamic state (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The WT-mutant mix showed even lower chaperone activity, underlining the dominant-negative role of HspB8-K141E mutant over the WT.
source: Remarkably, the WT-mutant mix showed even lower chaperone activity, underlining the dominant-negative role of HspB8-K141E mutant over the WT (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The HspB8-K141E mutant showed an increased number of inter-links with FUSm in condensates compared to HspB8-WT.
source: In comparison to HspB8-WT, the mutant showed an increased number of inter-links with FUSm in condensates, which suggests a stronger interaction between FUSm and the HspB8-K141E mutant (Figure 6E, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Almost all mono-links within the RRM domain of FUSm were decreased upon binding of the HspB8-K141E mutant.
source: A quantitative analysis revealed that almost all mono-links within the RRM domain of FUSm were decreased upon binding of the HspB8-K141E mutant, suggesting that accessibility to these sites was hindered (Figure 6F, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative XL-MS data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Multiple intra-links within HspB8 bridging the N-terminus to the αCD domain were increased in the HspB8-K141E mutant.
source: Concomitantly, multiple intra-links within HspB8 bridging the N-terminus to the αCD domain were increased in the HspB8-K141E mutant (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative XL-MS data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The increased intra-links in HspB8-K141E are in line with a potential conformational change of the chaperone mutant upon FUS binding that brings these domains closer to each other.
source: an observation that is in line with a potential conformational change of the chaperone mutant upon FUS binding that brings these domains closer to each other (Sailer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from XL-MS data and supported by citation to prior literature on interpreting XL-MS data.

claim: HspB8 uses its disordered domain to partition into liquid FUS condensates.
source: We show that HspB8 uses its disordered domain to partition into liquid FUS condensates
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from partitioning experiments with HspB8 truncation variants.

claim: HspB8 uses a similar molecular grammar as described previously for FUS.
source: and that HspB8 uses a similar molecular grammar as described previously for FUS (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Arginine residues in the IDR of HspB8 interact with tyrosine residues in the FUS-LCD.
source: More specifically, arginine residues in the IDR of HspB8 interact with tyrosine residues in the FUS-LCD, thereby promoting the targeting of the HspB8-αCD into FUS condensates for chaperoning of the misfolding-prone RRM domain of FUS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from partitioning experiments with HspB8 and FUS variants.

claim: Unfolding of the RRM drives FUS aging.
source: In this study, we take a biochemical approach using purified proteins to reconstitute a chaperone-mediated quality control mechanism associated with RNP granules and combine it with qXL-MS to probe PPIs inside condensates. We find that unfolding of the RRM drives FUS aging
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from aging assays and heat shock experiments.

claim: Interaction of the folded RRM with the sHSP HspB8 slows down the FUS aging process.
source: and that interaction of its folded RRM with the sHSP HspB8 slows down this aging process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from aging assays and FRAP experiments.

claim: RRM domains are small folded entities that bind to single-stranded RNA.
source: RRM domains are small folded entities that bind to single-stranded RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RRM domains.

claim: In humans, there are currently 745 RRM domains distributed over 446 proteins known to exist.
source: In humans, there are currently 745 RRM domains distributed over 446 proteins known to exist (Letunic and Bork, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cells use RNA to regulate condensate formation.
source: It has been proposed before that cells use RNA to regulate condensate formation (Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: RNA and HspB8 can compete for their interaction with FUS.
source: Our data suggests that RNA and HspB8 can compete for their interaction with FUS.
evidence: This is inferred from XL-MS data showing competition between RNA and HspB8.

claim: Some RRM domains require stabilization by binding to RNA.
source: While this requires experimental validation in future studies, we hypothesize that some RRM domains require stabilization by binding to RNA, and in cases where no RNA is available, the chaperone HspB8 takes over this function and protects the RRM domain from unfolding and aggregation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data presented.

claim: HspB8 has a general role in cell physiology in stabilizing RRM domains in condensates.
source: Thus, it is a possibility that HspB8 has a general role in cell physiology in stabilizing RRM domains in condensates.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Mutations in the genes coding for HspB1, HspB3, HspB5, and HspB8 have been associated with neuromuscular diseases.
source: To date, mutations in the genes coding for HspB1, HspB3, HspB5, and HspB8 have been associated with neuromuscular diseases (Vendredy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of the RRM slows down hardening but does not stop it.
source: Deletion of the RRM slows down hardening but does not stop it.
evidence: This is supported by aging assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Other driving forces such as aberrant LCD-LCD interactions may require other types of chaperone systems to prevent them.
source: This suggests other driving forces such as aberrant LCD-LCD interactions that may require other types of chaperone systems to prevent them.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that RRM deletion slows but does not stop aging.

claim: A changed environment after phase separation could destabilize folded domains and require chaperones to stabilize them.
source: A changed environment after phase separation could destabilize folded domains and require chaperones to stabilize them.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Such a mechanism would necessitate many domain-specific chaperones for stabilization inside condensates.
source: Such a mechanism would necessitate many domain-specific chaperones for stabilization inside condensates.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The crosslinker used throughout this manuscript will react with primary amines and thus primarily link lysine residues within studied proteins.
source: Please note that the crosslinker used throughout this manuscript, disuccinimidyl suberate (DSS), will react with primary amines and thus primarily link lysine residues within studied proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemistry of DSS crosslinker.

claim: The LCD of FUS contains no lysines.
source: It is important to remember that the LCD of FUS contains no lysines and therefore our approach is not picking up interactions between and amongst the LCD domains
evidence: This is a factual statement about the amino acid composition of the FUS LCD.

claim: The vast majority of changes in crosslinks are happening during the formation of fiber states.
source: A global view of all quantified crosslinking sites shows that the vast majority of changes are happening during the formation of fiber states (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved XL-MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Interactions between RRM domains and within RRM domains decrease as condensates age.
source: The general trend is for interactions between RRM domains and within RRM domains to decrease as condensates age.
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved XL-MS data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HspB8 has previously been localized to stress granules.
source: HspB8 has previously been localized to stress granules (Ganassi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There was no detectable interaction between HspB8 and FUSm under non-phase separating conditions.
source: To test for a potential interaction between HspB8 and FUSm in the dilute phase, protein-protein interactions of 33 nM FUSm and HspB8 (left panel) and Taf-15 (right panel) were assessed under non-phase separating conditions (500 mM KCl) by Microscale Thermophoresis (Jerabek-Willemsen et al., 2011). While FUSm tightly bound to the stress granule protein Taf-15 with a KD of 260 nM, there was no detectable interaction between HspB8 and FUSm, even at a chaperone concentration of 120 µM.
evidence: This is supported by thermophoresis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: FUSm tightly bound to the stress granule protein Taf-15 with a KD of 260 nM.
source: While FUSm tightly bound to the stress granule protein Taf-15 with a KD of 260 nM, there was no detectable interaction between HspB8 and FUSm, even at a chaperone concentration of 120 µM.
evidence: This is supported by thermophoresis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Only inter-links between the αCD of HspB8 and the RRM of FUSm were exclusively detected inside condensates.
source: However, only inter-links between the αCD of HspB8 and the RRM of FUSm were exclusively detected inside condensates.
evidence: This is supported by XL-MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Partitioning of lactalbumin into FUSm condensates is caused by unspecific interactions.
source: This suggests that in contrast to the HspB8: FUSm interaction, partitioning of lactalbumin into FUSm condensates is caused by unspecific interactions.

claim: Stabilizing aggregation-prone folded RNA-binding domains inside condensates by molecular chaperones may be a general mechanism to prevent aberrant phase transitions.
